q-39188.name: Question 1
q-39188.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 \\ 20 & 8\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}.$
q-39188.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 \\ 20 & 8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8+4\text{i} & -4 \\ 20 & 8+4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(-8+4\text{i}){x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 20{x}_{1}+(8+4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-2+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-2+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=4\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}=\frac{(-2+\text{i})(-2-\text{i})}{(1)(1)}=5.
$$

Question 1
?

Let v1=[a1b1] and v2=[a2b2] be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix A=[−8−4208]. Given that λ1=−4i is an eigenvalue of A, find the value of b1b2a1a2.

a
29
b
1
c
15
d
129

5

Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ1=−4i and

A−λ1I=[−8−4208]−[−4i00−4i]=[−8+4i−4208+4i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(−8+4i)x1−4x2=020x1+(8+4i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(−4i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

x2=(−2+i)x1

Hence, the general solution is given by

[x1(−2+i)x1],x1∈C.

Setting x1=1, we get the eigenvector

v1=[1−2+i].

On the other hand, since λ1=−4i is a complex eigenvalue of A, the second eigenvalue of A must be the complex conjugate of λ1. Therefore,

λ2=λ1―=4i.

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to λ2 is

v2=v―1=[1−2−i].

Therefore, we obtain

b1b2a1a2=(−2+i)(−2−i)(1)(1)=5.

q-81031.name: Question 2
q-81031.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
q-81031.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\sqrt{2}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{2}\text{i} & 2 \\ -3 & -2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\sqrt{2}\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-2}{2+\sqrt{2}\text{i}}=\frac{-2(2-\sqrt{2}\text{i})}{6}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{i}.$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=−2i, and

{(2+2i)x1+2x2=0−3x1+(−2+2i)x2=0.

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[x1−12(2+2i)x1],x1∈C.

Setting x1=−2, we get the eigenvector

v=[−22+2i].

Finally, ab=−22+2i=−2(2−2i)6=−23+23i.

q-81195.name: Question 3
q-81195.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
q-81195.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 5 \\ -4 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 5 \\ -4 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2+4\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(5)(5)}{(-2+4\text{i})(-2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

?

Given that v1=[a1b1] and v2=[a2b2] are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix A=[75−43], what is the value of a1a2b1b2?

a
14
b
−2
c
54

4

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the eigenvalues of A. To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0: det(A−λI)=0|7−λ5−43−λ|=0(7−λ)(3−λ)−(−4)(5)=021−7λ−3λ+λ2+20=0λ2−10λ+41=0

Using the quadratic formula, we get

λ=−b±b2−4ac2a=10±(−10)2−4(1)(41)2(1)=10±−642=10±8i2=5±4i.

Therefore, the eigenvalues are λ=5±4i.

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue λ1=5+4i. We have

A−λ1I=[75−43]−[5+4i005+4i]=[2−4i5−4−2−4i].

Hence, we get the system of linear equations {(2−4i)x1+5x2=0−4x1+(−2−4i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(5+4i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

x2=(−25+45i)x1

Hence, the general solution is given by

[x1(−25+45i)x1],x1∈C.

Setting x1=5, we get the eigenvector

v1=[5−2+4i].

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to λ2=5−4i, we simply compute the complex conjugate of v―1, and get

v2=v―1=[5−2−4i].

Finally, a1a2b1b2=(5)(5)(−2+4i)(−2−4i)=54.

q-140385.name: Question 4
q-140385.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 10 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5-4\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
q-140385.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =5-4\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 10 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5-4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5-4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2+4\text{i} & 10 \\ -2 & 2+4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(-2+4\text{i}){x}_{1}+10{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+(2+4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5-4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=(1+2\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}(1+2\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1+2\text{i}}{1}=1+2\text{i}.$

{(−2+4i)x1+10x2=0−2x1+(2+4i)x2=0.

q-140388.name: Question 5
q-140388.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}?$
q-140388.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 4 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(4)(-5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-10)\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-10)\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 4 \\ -5 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+4\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-5)(-5)}{(2+4\text{i})(2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
